subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: joining a study group for accountability [Action]
passage: Coding club teacher's note, Friday. Samir has been meeting two classmates in the library every Friday at 4:15. The rule: each person solves one problem during the week and presents the solution to the other two. Week three was a dull one, with exams and heat, and I saw Samir skip. The others didn't scold. One sent a message: “We start at 4:15, need your loop.” Samir turned up with half a solution, and the three finished it together. Nobody has missed since. All I did was give them a corner and a whiteboard. Samir told me, “If it were only me, I'd have quit in week three.” — Zainab

qa.q: When does the study group meet?
What might Samir be feeling when admitting to quitting in week three without the group?
qa.a: Grateful and a bit relieved: the group's nudge kept Samir going through a dull week.

qa.q: What else could the group do to keep going, and why?
qa.a: Take turns choosing the weekly problem, since shared ownership keeps everyone invested.

qa.q: How does the group look to the classmate who sent the message?
qa.a: That classmate probably feels responsible for the group and glad Samir came, and the kind nudge kept it friendly instead of scolding.

grounding: A student teams with two classmates to solve and present one problem a week and nudge whoever skips.

passage:
Friday
Third Friday of the plan and I nearly skipped it. The deal Maria, Sunny and I made: one problem a week from the practice site, everyone solves it alone, and on Friday after school we each show our solution on Maria's tablet in the library, five minutes each.
This week's problem was about reversing words. I left it till Thursday night and got stuck. I was going to text them that I was ill. Then Maria messaged, “Tejas, you alive? Friday! 🙂” Annoying. But it worked.
I showed my half-solution anyway. Sunny had done it a totally different way, with a loop running backwards. Maria's was the shortest. I felt a bit resentful that both of them finished, but seeing three ways to solve one thing taught me more than a whole video.
Next week's problem is already copied into my notebook.

qa.q: What was this week's problem about?
How did Tejas feel on seeing that Maria and Sunny had both finished?
qa.a: Tejas felt a bit resentful, yet found that seeing three different solutions taught more than a whole video.

qa.q: What could the three add so a stuck member doesn't think of pretending to be ill?
qa.a: A mid-week check-in, like a one-line "where are you stuck?" message on Tuesday, would let help arrive before Friday.

qa.q: How might Maria see that nudge message?
qa.a: Maria may feel like the one keeping the group honest; the friendly nudge kept Tejas from quietly dropping out that week.

grounding: Shows three students solving one problem a week, presenting on Fridays and nudging whoever is slipping, which keeps them going.
